newsitem.title: USA: U.S. psychologists delay award, weigh racism charge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. psychologists delay award, weigh racism charge.

text.p: The leading group of U.S. psychologists said Friday it would delay giving an award to a major figure in the field in order to judge his work and review his statements that critics have condemned as racist.

The planned presentation Saturday of a lifetime achievement award to psychologist Raymond Cattell, 92, at the American Psychological Association's annual meeting was cancelled earlier this week, spokeswoman Rhea Farberman said.
Criticisms of the British-born Cattell, who spent most of his career in the United States, published on the Internet said he made unretracted anti-Semitic statements in the 1930s.

Cattell's critics, who included Ferris State University historian Barry Mehler, said he was a strong believer in eugenics who thought that a growing number of less-intelligent people should be discouraged from having children.
Cattell is known primarily for his work in IQ and personality testing and has authored some 41 books.
He also founded what some have described as a new religious movement, "Beyondism," which is based on eugenics.
Cattell was understandably disappointed when told of the controversy, Farberman said. He has said his views on eugenics have evolved.
A blue-ribbon panel of psychologists would likely take several months to review Cattell's work, Farberman said.
"We need to investigate his work and see if the criticisms of him have been taken out of context, and judge whether the quotes (attributed to Cattell) are accurate," Farberman said.
"We need to make a determination if the accusations of racism are valid and if they influenced the science," she said.
